title: Review 86: Rethinking Curriculum Enhancement and Strategic Provision 2026
author: Chris Jones
summary: Chris Jones, writing for the SMARTcurriculum network, argues that school leaders must become far more precise about the relationship between curriculum provision, teacher time and learner need. He distinguishes baseline provision, the minimum entitlement funded by the learners in the organisation, from enhancement, the deliberate investment of extra teacher-led time above that baseline. His claim is that enhancement should never be accidental, and that comparative staffing metrics such as contact ratios often obscure rather than explain educational design. He warns that incremental, reactive additions accumulate into workload, cost, timetabling complexity and fragmentation, and he links enhancement to inclusion by asking how teacher-led provision can be strengthened so more pupils succeed within it rather than being extracted. The thread running through the piece is that curriculum leadership is system leadership, and that the goal is coherence rather than either expansion or cost cutting.
points: Leaders should be able to say where enhancement sits, why it exists, what value it creates and whether it is sustainable, because unplanned enhancement quietly outpaces organisational coherence.
Benchmarking against comparative staffing metrics invites designing for comparability instead of purpose; the better question is what educational experience the school is intentionally designing.

Strengthening teacher-led provision through co-teaching, flexible grouping and timetable redesign can improve inclusion more than extraction models, though it demands more organisational sophistication.
Curriculum is organisational architecture: decisions about it shape staffing, workload, wellbeing and culture, so curriculum leaders need systems thinking as well as pedagogy.
quotes: That distinction matters enormously because enhancement should never be accidental. It should represent deliberate educational choice. A school may decide to enhance provision because learners require additional support, class structures need adaptation, curriculum pathways require greater flexibility, staffing expertise allows broader access to the curriculum, or inclusion priorities demand additional teacher-led intervention.

The danger is that schools begin designing provision primarily around comparability rather than purpose. At #SMARTcurriculum, we try to shift the conversation away from simple comparison and toward strategic articulation. The more important question is not “How do we compare?” but “What educational experience are we intentionally designing, and how are we deploying resources to achieve it?

Over time, I have found that the strongest schools are rarely those with the most resources overall. More often, they are the schools that understand precisely where additional investment creates the greatest value for learners.

Traditionally, many schools responded to learner difficulties through extraction models, in which pupils were removed from teacher-led curriculum experiences for intervention elsewhere. In some cases, that remains appropriate and necessary.
Individually, each decision may feel entirely reasonable. Collectively, schools can unintentionally create systems in which enhancement outpaces organisational coherence.

This is why effective curriculum leaders increasingly need systems thinking as well as pedagogical expertise. They must understand not only what learners need educationally, but how organisational structures either enable or constrain those experiences.
Sustainable schools are not built through endless expansion. They are built through thoughtful alignment between vision, provision, staffing and capacity.

Ultimately, the goal of understanding enhancement is neither to reduce ambition nor to reduce cost. The goal is coherence. Schools need clarity around what baseline provision looks like, where enhancement exists, why enhancement matters, whether enhancement aligns with organisational purpose and whether enhancement remains sustainable.
